entries.title: 2 killed, 1 hurt in Amtrak train crash in Western Springs
entries.summary: <p>An Amtrak train collided with a vehicle Wednesday morning at a railway crossing in west suburban Western Springs, leaving two people dead and at least one injured. </p><p>At 8 a.m., Amtrak train No. 381, westbound from Chicago to Quincy, hit a vehicle on the tracks at Wolf Road in Western Springs, according to Amtrak and a statement from the village of Western Springs, about 20 miles west of Chicago. No other details were provided, such as whether the crossing arms were lowered at the time of the collision.</p><p>Two people in the vehicle were killed, and another person was transported to Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, according to the statement. </p><p>The Cook County medical examiner's office had not released their names or other details as of noon Wednesday.</p><p>None of the 35 passengers and crew were hurt, Amtrak said.</p><p>Train customers were moved to a bus to continue west, with that bus making all of the regular train stops between La Grange and Quincy, according to Amtrak. </p><p>Several law enforcement and emergency response teams were on site as the investigation continues. </p><p>Crossings at Grand Avenue and Wolf Road are closed, but Lawn Avenue remains open. All traffic and pedestrians should avoid the area until further notice. </p><p>Those tracks are also used by Metra's BNSF line, which announced significant cancellations, warning passengers that crowding on remaining trains could be severe and to plan on alternate transportation if possible, according to the Metra website. A Metra spokesperson said that while the tracks were fine and some trains had passed through Wednesday night, crew rest hour requirements could carry over delays into early Thursday, though service would likely be close to normal.</p><p>As a result, inbound and outbound BNSF trains would travel only between Union Station and La Grange Road, and between Aurora and Hinsdale. No train service will be provided between Stone Avenue and Highlands, according to a service alert on the Metra website.</p><p>As of Wednesday night, Western Springs had not provided any updates on the accident.</p>

entries.title: Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson answers the bell ... at least until 2nd half
entries.summary: <p>The growing pains continue for Caleb Wilson.</p><p>At least on Wednesday, literally.</p><p>The Bulls’ prized rookie was questionable to answer the bell against the Spurs, dealing with a sore hip in the wake of the loss to Philadelphia on Sunday. It was enough of a concern that he needed to get through warmups, test it out, and then give the medical staff the nod that he was good to go.</p><p>He did play well in his 15 minutes of work, scoring 15 points on 5-of-7 shooting, but injured his right hand and did not return to the game in the second half.</p><p>A reminder to the Bulls that leading the team with 32.4 minutes per game was necessary for the development piece that the No. 4 overall draft pick needs, but maybe a stat they want to keep a little closer eye on for the next few games.</p><p>“We’ve got to be smart with him of course,” coach Tiago Splitter said of Wilson. “He’s playing a lot of minutes. Those minutes are important to his development, but we’ve also got to be smart with his body being young. I think there’s a false thought that when you’re young you can do whatever but that’s not true. You’ve got to get stronger, you’ve got to get your body prepared to face a season like the NBA, so we’ve got to be careful there and we’ve got to monitor it for sure.”</p><p>Wilson played 32 minutes against the 76ers and was coming off a game in New York in which he had a soft benching in New York because of body language and a lack of resiliency in Splitter’s estimation. He only put in a season-low 22 minutes in that loss until leaving the Spurs game early.</p><p>But even with those moments for the 20-year-old where he might take one step back, there’s been way more moments of taking steps forward through the first 10 games.</p><p>“Honestly every game is a little bit different,” Splitter said of the Wilson’s growth so far. “He did some great things, and other games he wasn’t as good, but again, it’s not like a (upward) line. It’s up and down, up and down, and you grow, right. I think he’s working hard, he’s doing everything we ask. There are a lot of things on his plate right now, learning different things, and he’s grown, he’s getting better.”</p><p><b>The Claxton Effect</b></p><p></p><p>The sample size is small – just two games to be exact – but veteran big man Nic Claxton’s presence was being felt on both ends of the floor.</p><p>Claxton, who was acquired in an offseason four-team trade, was sidelined since the start of training camp with a strained hamstring. He made his Bulls debut in the Sunday loss to the 76ers, coming off the bench because of minutes restrictions, and was again in that role against San Antonio.</p><p>One player that’s really appreciated having Claxton behind him protecting the rim? Second-year forward Noa Essengue.</p><p>“That’s one of the best feelings, honestly,” Essengue said. “Because I know I can make a mistake because I have someone behind me to protect me, so it’s just amazing.</p><p>“I just know I can do a little more. I can put a little more pressure on the ball, try more deflections.”</p><p></p><p><b>A vet down</b></p><p></p><p>Norman Powell missed his second consecutive game, still dealing with back spasms.</p><p>The good news for the Bulls and their veteran shooting guard? It doesn’t sound like he’ll be in street clothes much longer.</p><p>“He’s around 70%, not ready to go, but expecting him to be ready next game,” Splitter said.</p><p>With Powell sidelined, the Bulls again turned to veteran wing Isaac Okoro. Okoro also started Sunday’s game against the 76ers, finishing with 12 points and a plus-1 in plus/minus.</p>

entries.title: Taking care of business: Chicago's first self-cleaning public restroom opens in Polish Triangle
entries.summary: <p>Christian Malatesta wanted to go first.</p><p>When he heard the 1st Ward, where he lives, was getting Chicago's first self-cleaning public restroom, Malatesta emailed Ald. Daniel La Spata to ask for the first spot in line.</p><p>Malatesta, 35, had used a similar facility in Paris, and was excited to see the technology come to Chicago.</p><p>“I don't think you should have to buy a $5 cup of coffee to use the restroom,” he said.</p><p>His big moment arrived Wednesday, when La Spata and JCDecaux, the company providing and operating the facility, officially opened it to the public.</p><p>Located near the CTA's Division Street Blue Line station, the facility is designed for one user at a time. Visitors press a button to open the sliding door. Inside, there's a bright blue wall and a map of Chicago and plenty of space to move about comfortably. When they've left, an integrated system washes and disinfects the toilet and floor after each use.</p><p>Malatesta got his wish, and headed in. The experience, he said, was straightforward.</p><p>“Everything was labeled very clearly, and everything was where I expected it to be,” Malatesta said. “You just press the button, the door opens for you, it flushes for you.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-280000" name="image-280000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ba04b4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0618aea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4582bd6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F15%2Fe4%2Faa37d56d4975b51b827a77d3ad52%2Fwesttowntoilet-261112-18.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. entries.title: What to know about CPS and AI as Chicago students risk losing access to Google search
entries.summary: <p>It's AI’s world and we’re just living in it.</p><p>At least that’s what the last couple of years have felt like as artificial intelligence creeps into gadgets, software, media and other aspects of our lives. Some school districts, such as New York and Los Angeles, have responded by banning AI for some students.</p><p>In Chicago Public Schools, students aren’t allowed access to popular AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google’s Gemini and other generative AI programs because of privacy and safety concerns.</p><p>But that doesn’t mean teachers and students aren’t using AI. The school district has released guidance for educators and students for the last two years on how they can adopt the technology in teaching and learning. The guidance says it prioritizes “human oversight” while promoting and encouraging “experimentation” of district-approved AI tools to enhance what students get out of the classroom.</p><p>The framework gives students examples of how to use the technology, such as creating study guides and generating images about a chapter of a book they are reading. It suggests ways teachers can use AI to get rid of “busy work” and spend more time with students.</p><p>At the same time, a growing chorus of parents want to put the brakes on the district’s embrace of AI and minimize screen time for students, citing concerns that it could be affecting their learning.</p><p>As the district continues to grapple with the fast-evolving technology it also has to deal with a new issue. Last week <a class="Link" href="https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/ai-learning-era-updates-2026/" target="_blank" ><u>Google announced</u></a> that next year school districts that choose to forego its AI products will lose access to Google search.</p><p>That puts CPS in a major bind and helped fuel a protest in front of Google’s West Loop office on Wednesday. Students use Google search for homework, research and other assignments. The district also relies on other Google products, such as Google Classroom, Google Drive and Google Docs. Finding alternatives would be a big undertaking.</p><p>Here are a few things to know about the district’s approach to AI.</p><p><b>Why are Chicago Public Schools students at risk of losing Google search?</b></p><p>Earlier this month Google <a class="Link" href="https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/ai-learning-era-updates-2026/" target="_blank" ><u>announced updates to its suite of programs</u></a> that use AI, including Google Classroom and Gemini Notebook, an AI research tool. Access will be automatically turned off for K-12 students until administrators turn them on.</p><p>But Chris Phillips, vice president of education at Google, in <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/google-search-schools-restrict-ai.html?unlocked_article_code=1.NlE.VMKr.Cr-g-C6phyfH&smid=url-share" target="_blank" ><u>an interview with the New York Times</u></a>, said that schools that ban AI entirely “will not have access to search” because “search and AI are deeply engrained.”</p><p>The district has “not yet determined its response to Google's announced search engine restriction,” a CPS spokesperson said in a statement.</p><p>CPS is “actively exploring all options to independently suppress” the AI mode amid those constraints, the statement said. “The District would like to continue to provide students with access to the Google search engine without the AI component. If such an arrangement can’t be reached, the District will look to other search solutions.”</p><p>In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the company is updating its AI search features for classrooms so it gives step-by-step instructions on how to solve problems instead of just “quick answers.” The statement didn’t address the protest or answer questions about cutting off search.</p><p>New York and LA, which enacted strict restrictions on AI use in schools, are in the same boat as Chicago. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said “no corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”</p><p>Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. In addition to its suite of programs, CPS also invested in Google Chromebooks which are now heavily integrated with Gemini, Google’s AI assistant</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>What do we mean when we talk about AI?</b></p><p>In general, whenever someone discusses AI in schools they are referring to Generative AI, a subset of artificial intelligence that generates new content such as text, audio, code, images or video. These outputs are based on data that is typically derived from the internet.</p><p>Users input specific requests via text prompts to generate the content. This usually takes the form of a chatbot. Popular programs include Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini.</p><p><b>What is CPS’ AI policy?</b></p><p>The district doesn’t have a binding policy on the use of the technology within CPS. Instead, the district <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/globalassets/cps-pages/initiatives/ai-guidebook/cps-ai-guidebook.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>has released guidelines</u></a> for educator use in their classrooms. CPS has said it chose to first develop guidance rather than policy because that gave it the flexibility to adapt to the fast-evolving nature of the technology.</p><p>The district released its first version in 2024, around the time AI chatbots were becoming more widely used. It was among the first districts in the state to release guidance. The guidelines have been updated several times but the core principles have remained the same.</p><p>They aim to ensure that “AI augments, rather than replaces, the essential role of educators.” The district has an online database of approved AI tools. Teachers that use the tools are also responsible for monitoring how students are using them.</p><p>That means that staff have to review any results from an AI tool for accuracy or biases. The guidelines also advise staff to only enter confidential information — such as student records and any identifying information — into AI tools that have privacy agreements with the district.</p><p>This year the district released a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/globalassets/cps-pages/initiatives/ai-guidebook/instructional-genai-playbook.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>“GenAI Playbook”</u></a> that provides examples of how teachers can use the technology. It recommends teachers think about “busy work” that AI can help with so they have more time with students. It suggests teachers use AI to help draft progress reports, incident logs or put together meeting minutes.</p><p>The playbook also includes ways teachers can integrate approved AI tools in their lessons. For example, teachers can use AI to create an interactive podcast version of a textbook chapter and have students chime in.</p><p><b>How are students using AI in the classroom? </b></p><p>That can depend on the school, the teachers, parents and the tools themselves. Currently students do not have direct access to AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s Gemini. The district blocks access to those tools on student accounts.</p><p>“With the exception of Google Search's default AI Mode, which the District is actively working to suppress, CPS does not provide students with access to generative AI applications in order to safeguard student privacy and safety,” a district spokesman said in a statement.</p><p>Parents can also opt their children out of having access to AI tools. Many tools also restrict access for younger students. ChatGPT and Perplexity don’t allow anyone under 13, for example.</p><p>According to the CPS guidelines, students first must get permission from their teacher before using AI tools for academic work and identify any AI-generated content in their assignments. The district reserves the right to take away access to these tools from students who use them irresponsibly.</p><p>The recent AI playbook suggests AI can help with brainstorming, generating timelines and tasks for group projects as well as overcoming writer’s block.</p><p>Students may also use AI to create videos, music and digital media with AI to compliment their learning. One example is for students to use a district-approved tool to create an image based on a chapter of a book they are reading.</p><p>The implementation of this guidance can vary depending on how comfortable teachers are with the technology. Some teachers may welcome the tools, while others may be more reluctant.</p><p>But the guidance doesn’t prevent students from interacting with AI at home. The district’s guidebook acknowledges that, and asks teachers to consider showing students how to responsibly interact with the technology.</p><p><b>Why are some parents asking for a moratorium on AI at CPS?</b></p><p>Google’s announcement also prompted swift backlash from groups that want CPS to enact a 3-year moratorium on AI use in schools and are seeking to limit screen time in classrooms.</p><p>Illinois Families for Public Schools and the local chapter of Schools Beyond Screens held a protest outside Google’s West Loop office on Wednesday. They are also calling on CPS to develop a more clear and consistent policy on AI and for the district to limit screen time in all grades.</p><p>Kimberly Tobin, parent of two young children at Burroughs Elementary, said Google’s announcement felt “like an ultimatum” for school districts.</p><p>“It's more influence than I would like tech companies to have over the types of products that are put in front of our kids,” she said.</p><p>Tobin said research indicates that increased screen time and unrestricted use of AI can affect student’s grades and keep them from developing skills.</p><p>“There's a pretty significant risk of fragmented attention when kids are doing most of their work on a screen,” Tobin said.</p><p>She and Schools Beyond Screens want CPS to look at how technology use impacts learning and develop a clear policy so that AI use doesn’t vary from school to school.</p><p>She noted that while the district restricts use of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude from students, some of the approved education programs, such as reading assistant Amira, use AI.</p><p>“It's not like we don't want them to have access to any kind of technology, but we want it to be for a purpose,” Tobin said.</p>

entries.title: Bears sending care package after viral social media interaction
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> are sending a care package to an Australian X user after Bears fans reached out in their time of need.</p><p>On Sunday, a social media user by the name of @treatmachanwell wrote a dark post on X: “If I kill myself then I'm just no longer a burden.” Later that night, Bears fans went to the app to search for medical updates on wide receiver Luther Burden, who was concussed on a fumble the fourth quarter. By searching the word “Burden,” they were fed the post. </p><p>Almost 500 people responded encouraging the user to stay upbeat. Many sent photos of Luther Burden or Bears fans inside Soldier Field — which was initially confusing to the social media user.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">HOW DID I GET THIS FAR <a href="https://t.co/naToKajBox">https://t.co/naToKajBox</a> <a href="https://t.co/2dhhekcySE">pic.twitter.com/2dhhekcySE</a></p>— ⋆˚࿔ 𝕐𝕦𝕣𝕚 ♪˚⋆ (@treatmachanwell) <a href="https://x.com/treatmachanwell/status/2120614751919300750?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“Ive got no idea who the Chicago Bears are — I'm Australian,” wrote Yuri, whose original post has more than 7 million views.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Extending a special welcome to all the newest members of Bears FC 🫶</p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2120591052361069018?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Wednesday, the user posted a screen shot of the Bears offering to mail a care package. The Bears even posted about the interactions themselves.</p><p>“Extending a special welcome to all the newest members of Bears FC,” the team wrote Wednesday, with an emoji of two hands forming a heart.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley
